items.item: Every correctness claim about a distributed protocol is relative to a system model: a protocol correct in one model can be wrong in another.

items.item: A synchronous system has known bounds on message delay and relative processor speed; an asynchronous system has none.

at.step: Reveal: three timing models, the same space-time diagram

items.item: Partial synchrony sits between them in two distinct forms: a bound that exists but is unknown, or a bound that only holds from some unknown global stabilization time (GST) onward.

at.step: Reveal: three timing models, the same space-time diagram

items.item: GST is unknown to the processors themselves — the model gives the protocol no way to detect that stabilization has happened.

at.deep: Internals: the model as a contract

items.item: A correctness condition splits into safety (never violated, whatever the timing) and liveness/termination (guaranteed only once the timing bound holds); the GST model is exactly equivalent to requiring safety always and termination only after GST.

at.deep: Internals: the model as a contract

items.item: The classical fault hierarchy is crash-stop, omission and Byzantine, each containing the one before it; authenticated Byzantine sits between omission and unauthenticated Byzantine because forged signatures are ruled out.

at.step: Reveal: four fault classes, one hierarchy

items.item: Byzantine tolerance requires strictly more replicas for the same resiliency than crash or omission tolerance (3t+1 vs 2t+1) because a Byzantine replica can actively lie, not just go silent.

at.deep: Frontier: Byzantine's cost, and where it's actually paid

items.item: Crash-recovery (a process that restarts, possibly having lost its in-memory or even unflushed on-disk state) is a distinct, and in production more realistic, fault model that the classical DLS taxonomy does not itself include.

at.step: Reveal: four fault classes, one hierarchy

at.deep: Internals: the model as a contract

items.item: A fair-loss link only guarantees that a message retried infinitely often is eventually delivered; it may lose, reorder or duplicate any single attempt.

at.step: Reveal: a fair-loss link, and what turns it reliable

items.item: A reliable (perfect) link is not a property of real wires — it is fair-loss plus retransmission and deduplication built on top, engineered, not given.

at.step: Reveal: a fair-loss link, and what turns it reliable

items.item: "Timeout means crashed" is only a sound inference in a synchronous model; in a partially synchronous or asynchronous one a slow, live process and a crashed one are indistinguishable by timeout alone.

at.deep: Internals: the model as a contract

items.item: The Two Generals problem shows no protocol over a lossy channel, however many rounds of acknowledgement, can let both parties be certain the other received the final message — the reason every 'reliable' layer rests on an accepted residual risk, not a guarantee.

items.item: FLP shows deterministic consensus is impossible in a fully asynchronous system with even one crash fault — the reason every real consensus protocol either assumes partial synchrony or randomizes.
